props.title: A Pure Formality

sections.content: A Pure Formality (1994) stands as one of the most intriguing psychological thrillers of the 1990s, featuring a masterful performance by Gérard Depardieu as Onoff, a famous writer being interrogated by a mysterious police inspector (Roman Polanski). The film's claustrophobic interrogation room setting and circular narrative structure draws compelling parallels to other psychological chamber pieces like Identity (2003) and Memento (2000), while its metaphysical themes echo The Sixth Sense (1999). Director Giuseppe Tornatore, fresh off his success with Cinema Paradiso (1988), crafts a sophisticated puzzle box that questions reality, memory, and identity.

sections.content: The film's brilliant use of the unreliable narrator technique influenced later works like Fight Club (1999) and Mulholland Drive (2001). Tornatore's decision to cast Roman Polanski as the inspector adds meta-textual depth, given Polanski's own psychological thrillers like Death and the Maiden (1994). The rain-soaked atmosphere and cyclical structure create a purgatorial feeling that prefigures similar techniques in Jacob's Ladder (1990) and The Others (2001).

The interrogation framework serves as more than just a plot device - it becomes a metaphysical examination of artistic creation itself. This approach to creative consciousness can be traced through later films like Adaptation (2002) and Synecdoche, New York (2008), where the line between creator and creation becomes increasingly blurred. The film's ending, which subverts audience expectations, established a template for psychological twist endings that would become more prevalent in the late 1990s and early 2000s. sections.content: A Pure Formality helped establish several techniques that became hallmarks of sophisticated psychological thrillers: the unreliable protagonist, circular narrative structure, and ambiguous reality. These elements can be seen in later works like Inception (2010) and Shutter Island (2010). The film's influence extends to international cinema, particularly visible in Korean thrillers like Oldboy (2003) and French productions like Tell No One (2006).
